desc:
You are given two binary search trees, tree1 and tree2. Return an array containing the values of both trees in ascending order. A value that appears in both trees must appear twice in the result.

Inside one tree all values are distinct. Either tree may be empty. Aim for O(n + m) time without sorting the combined values.

Tree encoding. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level order. The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn, level by level, from left to right. A missing child is written as -1 (node values are never negative, so -1 cannot be confused with a value). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped. The empty tree is [].

For example, [5,2,7,-1,3,6] is the tree whose root 5 has left child 2 and right child 7; node 2 has no left child and right child 3; node 7 has left child 6 and no right child.

Example 1

tree1 = [4,2,6], tree2 = [5,1,7,-1,2]
Output: [1,2,2,4,5,6,7]
tree1 holds 2, 4, 6 and tree2 holds 1, 2, 5, 7.

Example 2

tree1 = [], tree2 = [3,1]
Output: [1,3]
constraints: 0 ≤ number of nodes in each tree ≤ 3,000
0 ≤ node value ≤ 100,000; values are distinct within each tree; both trees are valid BSTs
The two trees together have at least one node
hints: Putting both value lists together and sorting gives the answer in O((n + m) log(n + m)). Can you use the fact that each tree is already ordered?
An inorder traversal turns each tree into a sorted list.
Merge the two sorted lists with two pointers, always taking the smaller front element; on a tie take either (they are equal).
editorial: Each inorder traversal produces an ascending list in O(size) time, so the problem is the classic merge of two sorted lists. Keep one pointer in each list and repeatedly append the smaller front value, then append whatever remains of the other list.

The total cost is O(n + m) time and O(n + m) space for the lists and the result. If memory mattered, you could run both inorder traversals lazily with two stacks (one iterator per tree) and merge on the fly, which needs only O(h1 + h2) extra space beyond the output.
